title: AAMI driver app could drop claims by $4.2m
full_text:
Suncorp has forecast a $4.2m annual reduction in motor insurance claims off the back of its AAMI Driving Test campaign, which challenged people to test their driving skills resulting in improved road safety.
The campaign, which attracted half a million participants to use the program through the AAMI app, delivered a 9 per cent improvement against the business’ forecast claims reduction target.
The app monitors and analyses drivers’ behaviours to provide feedback. Mim Haysom the executive general manager of brand and customer experience of AAMI owner Suncorp told The Australian the campaign exceeded all of its targets, generating nearly 140,000 app downloads, 34 per cent above target, while 500,000 people visited the website, 20 per cent above expectations.
The campaign is part of Suncorp’s broader strategy of making prevention and resilience central to its business and empowering its customers – and non-customers – to take action in a long-term drive to reduce claim costs.
“When we launched the campaign, like with all of our prevention and resilience campaigns, we wanted to democratise the IP and give everyone access to tools to help them in the prevention space, given it’s one of our strategic pillars,” Ms Haysom said.
“What we saw was 27 per cent of the participants in the AAMI driving test were not AAMI customers. So they engaged with the brand, downloaded the app, even though they weren’t necessarily our customers – so more than a quarter of the people that took part in it.
“The ultimate aim is a reduction in accidents within our customer base and those using the app, and a reduction in claims costs because that helps with affordability more broadly.” While the campaign is reducing accident claims, it also served as a brand building exercise, delivering an 18 per cent lift in brand consideration, while research conducted by Ipsos found 85 per cent of respondents agreed the initiative made them view AAMI as a leader in road safety. Most significantly for the business, 61 per cent said the campaign had motivated them to drive more safely because safer behaviour was recognised and rewarded through the app.
The AAMI Safer Driving app is also providing the brand with access to a trove of driving behaviour data, through the insurer’s telematics technology. The app, which first launched in 2022, has captured more than one billion kilometres of driving data.
The longer-term commercial opportunity could lie in the data, which may provide AAMI insurers with significant driver behaviour analysis and measure the impact of road safety interventions.
It points to an increasingly data-driven approach to insurance, with Suncorp seeking to influence driving behaviour before accidents happen, rather than relying solely on claim management and repair costs after an incident.
That focus sees the AAMI campaign sit alongside Suncorp insurance’s award-winning marketing initiatives such as Resilience Road and Haven, which have focused on home protection against climate and environmental threats.
The AAMI strategy, which is driven by Ms Haysom and the company’s creative agency Leo Australia, aims to create significant behaviour change.
The campaign is built around an insight that 90 per cent of people believe they are above-average drivers, which presented an opportunity to use competition to challenge that confidence.
“Everyone thinks they’re a good driver and they’re the best driver on the road and it’s everyone else’s fault,” said Leo Australia’s chief creative officer Andy Fergusson.
The campaign tapped into that competitive instinct and used the app to provide motorists with evidence of their driving performance.
Leo Australia’s executive strategy director Mitch Hunter said: “The app became the tool that they couldn’t refute so for the first time they could see evidence of how they drove and where they needed to see improvement.” The data showed particularly strong improvements among motorists who initially recorded the lowest driving scores.
Drivers with scores below 50 out of 100 improved by an average of 18.5 points, while those scoring between 51 and 60 improved by an average of 13.5 points.
Among the lowest-scoring drivers, safe acceleration improved by 11 points, cornering by 11 points, responsible phone use by 6.5 per cent and speeding by 2.5 per cent.
Ms Haysom said the ongoing ability to monitor driving behaviour through the app would allow the insurer to track whether those improvements were sustained.
The business plans to continue its driver rewards program, which offers discounts and other incentives to motorists who demonstrate safer driving and improve their scores, as a long-term commitment rather than a short-term marketing campaign.
The commercial imperative is significant for insurers facing pressure to manage motor claims costs and maintain insurance affordability.
While the ultimate measures of success would be fewer accidents among customers and app users, lower claims volumes and reduced claims costs, Ms Haysom admits that broader economic conditions, such as the current high petrol prices, could also influence claim trends with drivers opting to drive less frequently to curb costs. Suncorp is currently working on developments to build on the campaign, with new research identifying different driving profiles and behaviours that could inform future engagement.
